newsitem.title: USA: Missouri row crops show stress from dry weather.
newsitem.headline: Missouri row crops show stress from dry weather.

text.p: The following is the weekly crop summary from the Missouri Agricultural Statistics Service for the week ended Sunday, August 3.

Row crops and pastures are showing the effects of the continued dry weather over most of the State. Scattered showers in some areas and a few days of below normal temperatures provided some relief for crops, but the general moisture shortage is limiting growth and causing stress to all crops. An average of 6.2 days were suitable for fieldwork during the week of Saturday, July 26th through Friday, August 1st.

The topsoil moisture supply was rated as 23 percent very short, 49 percent short, 27 percent adequate and 1 percent surplus, similar to the previous week. All districts continue to indicate significant topsoil moisture shortages.
Pasture and range condition is rated as, 6 percent very poor, 29 percent poor, 46 percent fair, 18 percent good and 1 percent excellent, a moderate decrease from the previous week.

Seventy-two percent of all soybeans are blooming or beyond and twenty-nine percent of the crop has begun setting pods. Development is about 5 days ahead of last year and the 6 days ahead of the 5-year average when 61 percent was blooming or beyond and the State is slightly ahead of the normal 26 percent setting pods. Development is most advanced in the northwestern and north-central districts with 94 and 88 percent blooming respectively, followed by the central third of the State at about 75 percent. Soybean condition is rated as, 5 percent very poor, 20 percent poor, 43 percent fair, 27 percent good, and 5 percent excellent, a general decline from a week ago.

Ninety-five percent of the corn crop is silking or beyond and forty-five percent has reached the dough stage. Development is ahead of the 5-year average of 79 percent silking or beyond and 41 percent in the dough stage, but slightly behind the 51 percent reaching the dough stage last year. Corn silking is virtually complete in all areas except in the northeastern district where 20 percent remains to be silked. Corn condition for the State is rated as, 5 percent very poor, 19 percent poor, 38 percent fair, 32 percent good and 6 percent excellent, a significant decline from the previous week. The crop is showing the effects of the moisture shortage as many of the driest fields are firing, especially on the lower portions of the plants.

Sixty-one percent of the grain sorghum crop is heading or beyond and five percent of the crop is coloring. Heading is 5 days ahead of last year and 4 days ahead of the normal for this date. Heading ranges from 33 percent in the central district to over 70 percent in the north-central, southwestern and southeastern districts. Coloring is the same as last year. Coloring is most advanced in the north-central district with 10 percent, followed by the south-central and southeastern districts at 9 and 7 percent respectively. Grain sorghum condition is rated as, 5 percent very poor, 13 percent poor, 43 percent fair, 34 percent good and 5 percent excellent, a slight decline from a week ago.

Eighty-five percent of the cotton crop is setting bolls, 10 days behind last year's average of 99 percent and 4 days behind the 5-year average of 93 percent. Cotton condition is rated as 5 percent very poor, 26 percent poor, 39 percent fair and 29 percent good and 1 percent excellent, as dry weather forced a significant decline from last week. Twenty-nine percent of the third crop of alfalfa has been cut, compared to 22 percent a year ago and 21 percent normally. Ninety-five percent of the other hay crop has been cut, compared to 92 percent a year ago and 89 percent for the 5-year average by this date.

Temperatures during the past week averaged from 3 degrees below normal in Columbia to 1 degree above normal in Caruthersville. Precipitation for the week averaged 0.42 inch. The heaviest district average rainfall was in the southeastern district at 0.71 inch, while all other areas averaged from none to less than half an inch. Rainfall during July averaged 2.27 inches well below the 30-year average of 3.76 inches. The National Weather Service in St. Louis and the USDA-FSA County Offices provided weather
